subject: Ancient History
sub_topic: Major Harappan sites and their features

concepts.name: Mohenjo-daro: Urban Planning and Structural Features
key_dimensions: Grid-pattern street layout and its implications for civic planning
The 'Great Bath': construction materials (burnt brick, gypsum mortar, bitumen lining) and its ritual vs. civic purpose debate
The so-called 'Assembly Hall' and 'Granary' — contested identification and what it reveals about UPSC trap of assuming function from form
Distinction between the Citadel (western mound) and Lower Town (eastern mound) — stratified urban zoning

concepts.name: Harappa: Archaeological Significance and Unique Finds
key_dimensions: First site to be discovered (1921) by Daya Ram Sahni — significance in naming the civilization
Two rows of six granaries with working floors — comparison with Mohenjo-daro granary (single structure)
Evidence of a 'burial ground' (Cemetery R-37 and Cemetery H) and what Cemetery H culture indicates about a later, possibly post-Harappan phase
Sandstone male torso and the dancing figure — evidence for proto-artistic traditions and UPSC trap on attribution of finds to correct sites

concepts.name: Lothal: Port Town and Trade Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Located in Gujarat — only site with a dockyard (tidal dock) enabling maritime trade with Mesopotamia
Debate on whether the structure is actually a dockyard or a irrigation reservoir — S.R. Rao vs. critics
Evidence of a bead-making factory, Persian Gulf seals, and rice husk — unique trade and agricultural indicators
Double burial (male + female in same grave) — social/ritual practice unique to Lothal among Harappan sites

concepts.name: Kalibangan: Fire Altars and Pre-Harappan Continuity
key_dimensions: Located in Rajasthan on the banks of the Ghaggar (ancient Saraswati) river — geographical significance
Pre-Harappan ploughed field surface — earliest evidence of ploughing in the subcontinent
Fire altars on both the Citadel and Lower Town — used as evidence for ritual/religious practices; contrast with absence at Mohenjo-daro
Absence of a Great Bath — UPSC trap: not all Harappan cities had identical features, implying decentralized ritual practice

concepts.name: Dholavira: Water Conservation and Signboard Inscription
key_dimensions: Located in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat — unique three-part city division (Citadel, Middle Town, Lower Town), unlike the typical two-part division
Elaborate water harvesting and storage system — 16 reservoirs, reflecting adaptation to arid environment
Large inscription near the northern gate — largest Harappan inscription found; possible signboard use, though undeciphered
Stadium-like structure — unique among all Harappan sites; recent UNESCO World Heritage Site status (2021)

concepts.name: Rakhigarhi: Largest Harappan Site and Recent Genetic Studies
key_dimensions: Located in Haryana — now considered the largest Harappan site, surpassing Mohenjo-daro in area
2018 DNA study findings: IVC people had no Central Asian steppe ancestry, fueling the Out-of-India theory vs. Aryan Migration Theory debate
Evidence of paved roads, drainage systems, large cemeteries — confirms it as a major urban center
Ongoing excavations — UPSC trap on treating it as a fully understood site; much remains under study

concepts.name: Surkotada: Horse Bones and Fortification Evidence
key_dimensions: Located in Gujarat — one of the few sites with evidence of horse bones (disputed), used in debates about Aryan presence or indigenous horse domestication
Unique fortification style — the entire settlement (not just citadel) was fortified, unlike typical Harappan pattern
Burial practices with pot burials — distinct from other sites
UPSC trap: horse bones at Surkotada are contested by scholars like Meadow; do not treat as confirmed evidence

concepts.name: Banawali: Town Planning Anomalies and Unique Artifacts
key_dimensions: Located in Haryana on the Ghaggar plain — shows both pre-Harappan and mature Harappan phases
Lacks the standard east-west/north-south grid — road network is less regular, making it an exception to the 'uniform town planning' generalization
Evidence of a toy plough — only site (along with Kalibangan) with direct plough-related evidence
Good quality barley found in abundance — agricultural significance distinct from other sites

concepts.name: Chanhudaro: Craft Production and Absence of Citadel
key_dimensions: Located in Sindh (Pakistan) — the only major Harappan site without a citadel, challenging the universality of the 'citadel + lower town' model
Evidence of bead-making, shell-ornament, and bronze tool manufacturing — major craft production center
Inkwell and evidence of a cartwright's shop — rare evidence of specialized artisan quarters
Footprints of a dog chasing a cat preserved in a brick — trivial but frequently asked UPSC detail

concepts.name: Harappan Seals: Types, Materials, and Functions
key_dimensions: Predominantly made of steatite (soapstone) — square shape with a perforated boss on the reverse; distinction from Lothal's Persian Gulf seals (circular, button-type)
Unicorn as the most commonly depicted animal — significance in trade identification and religious symbolism
Script on seals remains undeciphered — Dravidian vs. Proto-Dravidian vs. Brahmi ancestor theories
Functional uses: trade/commerce identification, ownership marks, possibly amulets — UPSC trap on assuming a single function

concepts.name: Harappan Script: Nature, Directionality, and Decipherment Debate
key_dimensions: Boustrophedon style writing (right-to-left, then left-to-right alternately) inferred from seal evidence
Over 400 distinct signs identified — too many for an alphabet, too few for a logographic system; classified as logo-syllabic
Has NOT been deciphered — UPSC trap: no claim of decipherment is officially accepted; Asko Parpola's Dravidian hypothesis is prominent but unproven
Comparison with other undeciphered scripts (Linear A) — highlights the civilizational isolation problem for historians

concepts.name: Harappan Drainage System: Engineering and Civic Administration Implications
key_dimensions: Covered drains running along the streets with inspection holes — evidence of a public health-conscious administration
Houses had private wells and bathrooms connecting to the main drain — private-to-public drainage hierarchy
Contrast with contemporaneous Mesopotamian cities lacking comparable drainage — used to argue Harappan civic superiority
UPSC trap: the sophistication of drainage is used to infer a 'strong centralized state,' but no palace or temple has been found — the political structure remains unknown

concepts.name: Harappan Economy: Trade Networks and Standardized Weights
key_dimensions: Standardized cubical weights (chert/agate) following a binary and decimal system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) — evidence of regulated trade
Trade with Mesopotamia evidenced by Harappan seals found in Ur and Akkad; Mesopotamian texts refer to 'Meluhha' as the Indus region
Absence of coins — barter system supplemented by standardized weights and possibly commodity-based exchange
Lothal's dockyard and Sutkagendor (coastal outpost in Balochistan) as nodes in a maritime trade network

concepts.name: Harappan Religion: Symbols, Figurines, and the Absence of Temples
key_dimensions: Proto-Shiva (Pashupati seal from Mohenjo-daro) — seated figure surrounded by animals; interpreted as precursor to Shiva but contested
Mother Goddess terracotta figurines — found across sites; associated with fertility worship
No confirmed temple structure found — UPSC trap: fire altars at Kalibangan ≠ temple; the Great Bath may have been for ritual purification, not worship
Pipal tree worship suggested by seals — continuity with later Hindu traditions of sacred tree veneration

concepts.name: Decline of the Harappan Civilisation: Theories and Evidence
key_dimensions: Aryan Invasion Theory (Mortimer Wheeler) — skeletal remains at Mohenjo-daro as massacre evidence; now largely discredited
Climatic/ecological theory — drying up of the Ghaggar-Hakra (Saraswati) river system; supported by satellite imagery and geological data
Flood theory — Robert Raikes' argument of tectonic uplift causing repeated flooding at Mohenjo-daro
UPSC trap: decline was gradual and multi-causal, not a single event; 'de-urbanization' rather than 'destruction' is the preferred academic framing

concepts.name: Geographical Distribution of Harappan Sites: Core vs. Peripheral Zones
key_dimensions: Core zone: Sindh, Punjab (Pakistan), Rajasthan, Haryana — densely packed sites along Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra systems
Peripheral/outlier sites: Sutkagendor (Balochistan coast), Shortugai (Afghanistan), Daimabad (Maharashtra) — evidence of extensive reach
Southernmost site: Daimabad (Maharashtra); Northernmost: Manda (Jammu); Easternmost: Alamgirpur (UP); Westernmost: Sutkagendor
UPSC trap: the civilisation is NOT confined to the Indus River — the Ghaggar-Hakra river belt had an equal or greater density of sites

concepts.name: Harappan Agriculture and Animal Husbandry: Crops and Domesticated Animals
key_dimensions: Crops: wheat, barley (staples), rice (Lothal and Rangpur), cotton (first known cultivation in the world), sesame, mustard
Domesticated animals: humped bull (Zebu), buffalo, sheep, goat, elephant, dog; pig evidence present
Horse controversy: claimed at Surkotada and Lothal but contested — critical for Aryan Migration debate
UPSC trap: cotton cultivation is attributed to the Harappans (not later cultures); also they did not use iron tools — Bronze Age civilization

concepts.name: Phases of Harappan Civilisation: Early, Mature, and Late
key_dimensions: Early Harappan (3500–2600 BCE): Pre-urban phase; sites like Mehrgarh (Balochistan) show Neolithic-to-Chalcolithic transition preceding IVC
Mature Harappan (2600–1900 BCE): Peak urban phase; all major cities flourished; standardized material culture across a vast area
Late/Post-Harappan (1900–1300 BCE): Cemetery H culture (Harappa), Jhukar culture (Sindh) — regional devolution and cultural simplification
UPSC trap: Mehrgarh is a pre-Harappan site (not a Harappan site per se) but is evidence of the agricultural antecedents of IVC

concepts.name: Harappan Art and Craft: Bronze Casting, Pottery, and Ornaments
key_dimensions: Dancing Girl (Mohenjo-daro) — lost-wax (cire perdue) bronze casting technique; represents both artistic and metallurgical sophistication
Pottery: wheel-made, predominantly red ware with black paintings; geometric and animal motifs — distinct from contemporaneous cultures
Bead-making industry: carnelian, lapis lazuli (imported from Badakhshan, Afghanistan), turquoise — evidence of long-distance trade
UPSC trap: lapis lazuli is NOT locally available and its presence confirms overland trade with Central Asia/Afghanistan, not just maritime trade

concepts.name: Harappan Burials and Social Structure: Evidence and Inferences
key_dimensions: Primary extended burials (head to north) with grave goods — pottery, ornaments placed alongside the dead
Absence of spectacular royal tombs (unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia) — suggests relatively egalitarian social structure or dispersed authority
Cemetery H culture burials show cremation and fractional burial — evidence of cultural transition/discontinuity in the later phase

UPSC trap: the lack of grand monuments or royal burials is used to argue against a 'priest-king' or theocratic model, though the Priest-King statue from Mohenjo-daro is often misrepresented as evidence of one
